name: Gashadokuro
description: Gashadokuro is a colossal skeletal Japanese yokai standing 10 or more meters tall, formed from the accumulated bones and rage of those who died of starvation, that prowls at night hunting travelers to devour.
full_description: Gashadokuro (餓者髑髏, 'starving skeleton') is a giant skeletal yokai from Japanese mythology, standing 10 or more meters tall and constructed from the skulls and bones of those who died of starvation or in battle without proper burial rites. Its eyes burn yellow or green. The creature produces a distinctive chattering sound — 'Gachi Gachi' — with its teeth, though it can also approach silently. It prowls at 2:00 a.m., hunting travelers to grab, crush, and devour. The only warning is a ringing in the ears that signals its approach. The foundational myth of the Gashadokuro centers on the 10th-century Japanese warrior Taira no Masakado, whose 939 rebellion (Tengyō no Ran) against the imperial government ended with his beheading by his cousin Taira no Sadamori and Fujiwara no Hidesato in 940. Masakado's daughter, Takiyasha Hime — a sorceress — retaliated by conjuring the first Gashadokuro from the bones of fallen soldiers to attack Kyoto. The creature dissipated only after Masakado's head was relocated to Shibasaki (modern Tokyo), where a shrine still exists near the Tokyo Imperial Palace. Shinto charms are said to ward off the creature. It dissipates once its accumulated rage is exhausted, causing skeletal collapse. The modern iconography of the Gashadokuro derives significantly from Utagawa Kuniyoshi's Edo-period ukiyo-e print Takiyasha the Witch and the Skeleton Spectre, though that print originally depicted multiple life-sized skeletons; the single-giant form was a later reinterpretation.
origin: A creature of Japanese mythology associated with the Kanto region and with sites of historical mass starvation or battlefield death. Most strongly associated with events in the Kanto area related to Taira no Masakado.

etymology.meaning: Gasha (餓者, starving person / one who died of hunger) + dokuro (髑髏, skull/skeleton) = 'starving skeleton' or 'skeleton of the starved'
etymology.first_use: The concept is rooted in 10th-century historical events; first appeared in print in the mid-20th century (Morihiro Saito, 1966)

timeline.event: Taira no Masakado launches the Tengyō no Ran rebellion against the imperial government in the Kanto region
timeline.significance: Historical events that form the mythological basis for the Gashadokuro legend
timeline.source: Japanese historical records; Wikipedia article on Gashadokuro

timeline.event: Taira no Masakado killed by Taira no Sadamori and Fujiwara no Hidesato; his daughter Takiyasha Hime allegedly conjures the first Gashadokuro from soldiers' bones
timeline.significance: The foundational mythological event of the Gashadokuro's origin

timeline.event: Morihiro Saito publishes an unnamed reference to the Gashadokuro in Bessatsu Shojo Friend
timeline.significance: Earliest documented print appearance of the Gashadokuro concept

timeline.event: Shigeru Mizuki features the Gashadokuro in Nakayoshi, referencing Utagawa Kuniyoshi's ukiyo-e print
timeline.significance: Key publication establishing the creature in modern yokai documentation

timeline.event: Arifumi Sato includes the Gashadokuro in Nihon Yokai Encyclopedia
timeline.significance: Encyclopedic codification of the creature in the yokai canon

related.name: Onryo
related.description: Japanese vengeful spirits; the Gashadokuro is formed from the collective rage of those who died starving

related.name: Gaki
related.description: Japanese hungry ghost; shares the starvation / hunger theme

cultural_notes: The Gashadokuro embodies the belief that those who die of starvation or battlefield violence without proper burial rites accumulate into a dangerous spiritual force. It serves as a reminder of the consequences of war, famine, and neglect of the dead.
